title: When VALESKA Became a Working Platform
description: The November 2025 decisions that turned VALESKA from an architecture into a working knowledge platform: non-destructive discovery, APQC, semantic search, and MCP.
body:
By November 29, 2025, VALESKA had crossed a useful threshold. It was no longer only an architecture described in a design document. The repository held a working foundation: a database designed for both structured records and semantic embeddings, a scanner, an APQC classifier, search services, and an MCP server through which an AI assistant could use those capabilities.

The record from this period is a set of design and implementation documents, not a transcript of every conversation. It nevertheless makes the questions clear. How can a system make a disordered body of files discoverable without forcing a disruptive migration? How can it preserve business context while allowing meaning-based search? And how can an assistant use the system without being made the keeper of the knowledge itself?

The decisions

The first decision was to index rather than rearrange. VALESKA would leave source files in their existing locations and create a knowledge layer around them. That protected established work patterns while making files available through metadata, classification, and search.

The second decision was to give the knowledge layer a shared vocabulary. The initial implementation used the APQC process classification framework to connect technical assets with business-process context. Classification could begin with understandable rules for paths, file types, and names, while leaving room for semantic and AI-assisted methods as the system matured.

The third decision joined exact structure with semantic discovery. PostgreSQL provided the durable relational record, while pgvector stored embeddings for similarity search. This made it possible to find material by a natural-language idea as well as by a filename, a keyword, or a taxonomy category.

The fourth decision was to make VALESKA available through standard interfaces. A command-line path supported direct use; the FastAPI service exposed application functions; and the Model Context Protocol server presented five initial tools to an AI assistant: search, classify, scan, list categories, and retrieve file information. The assistant could ask the system questions, but the platform retained the indexed record and its classifications.

What the implementation established

Phase 1 had established the core data models, PostgreSQL with pgvector, APQC classification, and a self-integration test in which VALESKA classified its own repository. Its recorded verification ran four tests successfully: data models, classification, database connectivity, and self-integration.

The Phase 2 milestone added the scanner, semantic, keyword, and hybrid search, file indexing, MCP tool registration, and integration tests. The implementation record reports five successful Phase 2 tests covering the MCP server, search engine, scanner, MCP tools, and their integration. The codebase also carried Docker configuration, environment-based configuration, and asynchronous processing so the design could move beyond a one-off demonstration.

This was the point at which the earlier architecture became testable behavior. A project could be scanned; files could be classified; their content could be indexed; and an AI assistant could call into a governed knowledge service rather than rely only on a temporary conversation.

What remained open

November 29 was a milestone, not a finished system. The next recorded phase was AI assistant integration and real-world validation. The important result was that the next question had changed. The work was no longer whether a value-stream knowledge architecture could be implemented. It was how a working platform should be applied, tested, and extended responsibly.

Historical basis: This entry is dated to the November 29, 2025 repository milestone, commit 8ff0b91, which records completion of the Phase 2 MCP development milestone. Its account is based on the contemporaneous software design document, implementation plan, README, and Phase 1 and Phase 2 implementation summaries. The Phase 2 summary contains an inconsistent internal month heading; the repository commit timestamp is used as the publication-date authority.
